## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

{{< include ../learning_objectives/0565-virtual-environments-r-renv-description.qmd >}}

## From implicit to explicit

In [Virtual environments: R (renv)](0560-virtual-environments-r-renv.qmd),
`renv` decided which packages to record by reading our code.
That is an **implicit** snapshot.
The project's code *is* its list of declared packages.

This book uses **explicit** snapshots instead.
The project lists the packages it needs in a file called `DESCRIPTION`,
and `renv::snapshot()` records those packages, and only those,
in `renv.lock`.
It is the same split `uv` uses,
where `pyproject.toml` declares and `uv.lock` locks.

Explicit snapshots work better for collaboration and container building:

- **The lockfile records what the project needs, not what any file happens to load.**
  An implicit snapshot scans every R file in the project,
  including a scratch script you wrote once to try a package.
  An explicit snapshot ignores them.
- **People can read `DESCRIPTION`.**
  It is a short list of packages with their versions,
  easy to check in a code review,
  where `renv.lock` lists every dependency of every package.
- **A container rebuilds exactly the declared set.**
  When the project is built from scratch,
  in a container or on a collaborator's computer,
  a package the code uses but the project never declared
  fails right there, instead of quietly working on your computer only.
  The container chapters rely on this.

We will switch the project from that chapter to explicit snapshots.
Its `analysis.R` loads two packages:

```{.r filename="analysis.R"}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

species_counts <- starwars |>
  count(species, sort = TRUE)
```

## The `DESCRIPTION` file

A `DESCRIPTION` file comes from R packages,
where it holds a package's name, version, and dependencies.
A data analysis project can use one too,
with `Type: project` to say it is not a package.

Here is the one
from the [docker-uv-renv](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv) example project
(MIT license), which the container chapters build on:

```{.default filename="DESCRIPTION"}
Type: project
Version: 2026.11.13
Description: The R packages this project uses. renv.lock locks them.
Depends:
    dplyr (== 1.2.1),
    ggplot2 (== 4.0.3),
    knitr (== 1.52),
    rmarkdown (== 2.32)
```

The `Depends` field lists the packages,
separated by commas,
each with an exact version in parentheses.
`(== 1.2.1)` is the R equivalent of the exact pins
in [uv: pinning exact versions](0545-virtual-environments-python-uv-exact-pins.qmd).

Our project starts by declaring only `dplyr`:

```{.default filename="DESCRIPTION"}
Type: project
Description: The R packages this project uses. renv.lock locks them.
Depends:
    dplyr (== 1.2.1)
```

## Switching to explicit snapshots

The snapshot type is a project setting:

```r
renv::settings$snapshot.type("explicit")
```

`renv` stores it in `renv/settings.json`,
which you commit,
so everyone on the project uses it:

```{.default filename="renv/settings.json"}
  "snapshot.type": "explicit",
```

Now take a snapshot:

```r
renv::snapshot()
```

```out
- The project is out-of-sync -- use `renv::status()` for details.
The following package(s) will be updated in the lockfile:

# CRAN -----------------------------------------------------------------------
- cpp11     [0.5.5 -> *]
- purrr     [1.2.2 -> *]
- stringi   [1.8.9 -> *]
- stringr   [1.6.0 -> *]
- tidyr     [1.3.2 -> *]

- Lockfile written to "~/Desktop/my_r_project/renv.lock".
```

`[1.3.2 -> *]` means the package was *removed* from the lockfile.
`renv` no longer reads `analysis.R`.
`DESCRIPTION` declares only `dplyr`,
so the snapshot dropped `tidyr` and the packages that came with it.

## The package you forgot to declare

This is the mistake explicit snapshots make possible,
and `renv::status()` does not catch it:

```r
renv::status()
```

```out
No issues found -- the project is in a consistent state.
```

From `renv`'s point of view, `DESCRIPTION`, `renv.lock`, and the project library agree.
`tidyr` is still installed on *your* computer,
so `analysis.R` still runs for you.

Your collaborator clones the project and runs `renv::restore()`,
which installs what `renv.lock` records.
Then they run the analysis from a terminal.
In R, `source("analysis.R")` does the same,
and on Windows it is the easier way,
because R's installer does not put `Rscript` on the Git Bash `PATH`.

```bash
Rscript analysis.R
```

```out
Error in library(tidyr) : there is no package called ‘tidyr’
Execution halted
```

To catch this yourself,
compare the packages your code uses with the ones `DESCRIPTION` declares.
`renv::dependencies()` lists the packages a file uses:

```r
renv::dependencies("analysis.R")$Package
```

```out
[1] "dplyr" "tidyr"
```

`tidyr` is not in `DESCRIPTION`.
The more reliable check is to run the analysis from a fresh environment,
which is what building and rendering in a container does in the container chapters.

## Adding a package: install, declare, snapshot

The fix is the loop you follow for every new package.
The README of the docker-uv-renv example project spells it out.

Install the package and look up the version you got:

```r
renv::install("tidyr")
```

```out
# Installing packages --------------------------------------------------------
✔ tidyr 1.3.2                              [linked from cache]
Successfully installed 1 package in 2.1 milliseconds.
```

```r
packageVersion("tidyr")
```

```out
[1] ‘1.3.2’
```

Declare it in `DESCRIPTION` with that version:

```{.default filename="DESCRIPTION"}
Type: project
Description: The R packages this project uses. renv.lock locks them.
Depends:
    dplyr (== 1.2.1),
    tidyr (== 1.3.2)
```

Before you snapshot,
`renv::status()` now reports that `tidyr` is declared but not recorded:

```r
renv::status()
```

```out
- The project is out-of-sync -- use `renv::status()` for details.
The following package(s) are in an inconsistent state:

 package installed recorded used
 cpp11   y         n        y
 purrr   y         n        y
 stringi y         n        y
 stringr y         n        y
 tidyr   y         n        y

See `?renv::status` for advice on resolving these issues.
```

With explicit snapshots, "used" means declared in `DESCRIPTION`,
or needed by a package that is.
`recorded` is `n` because `renv.lock` does not have them yet.
Snapshot to record them:

```r
renv::snapshot()
```

```out
- The project is out-of-sync -- use `renv::status()` for details.
The following package(s) will be updated in the lockfile:

# CRAN -----------------------------------------------------------------------
- cpp11     [* -> 0.5.5]
- purrr     [* -> 1.2.2]
- stringi   [* -> 1.8.9]
- stringr   [* -> 1.6.0]
- tidyr     [* -> 1.3.2]

- Lockfile written to "~/Desktop/my_r_project/renv.lock".
```

```r
renv::status()
```

```out
No issues found -- the project is in a consistent state.
```

Commit `DESCRIPTION` and `renv.lock` together.

## The same split as uv

| Job | `renv` with explicit snapshots | `uv` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Declare the packages, with exact versions | `DESCRIPTION`, `dplyr (== 1.2.1)` | `pyproject.toml`, `pandas==3.1.1` |
| Lock every package and dependency | `renv.lock` | `uv.lock` |
| Add a package | `renv::install()`, edit `DESCRIPTION`, `renv::snapshot()` | `uv add` (all three at once) |
| Check that the declared, locked, and installed packages match (not their versions) | `renv::status()` | `uv sync --check` |
| Recreate the environment | `renv::restore()` | `uv sync` |

`uv` never scans your code,
so it always behaves like an explicit snapshot.
With `renv`, the three steps of adding a package are separate,
and the declare step is the one that is easy to forget.
